what: Object.assign(target, ...sources) copies properties from one or more source objects onto a target object, and returns the target. It is a quick way to merge objects or to fill defaults.

It copies only own, enumerable properties (string keys and also Symbol keys). It reads each value from the source with a normal property read, so getters run, and it writes with a normal property write on the target, so setters run.
The copy is shallow. Nested objects are not cloned, only their references are copied.
Think of moving sticky notes from several boards onto one main board. Later boards win if two notes have the same label, and the main board is the one you get back.

steps: If the target is null or undefined, throw a TypeError. Otherwise turn it into an object.
Go through the sources in order. Skip null and undefined.
Turn each other source into an object (a string becomes an object with index keys).
List the source's own enumerable keys (strings and symbols).
For each key, read source[key] and write target[key] = value. Return the target.

where: Merge user options over defaults: Object.assign({}, defaults, options).
Create a changed copy of a small state object without touching the old one.
Copy helper methods from one object onto another.
Deep structures. Nested objects stay shared, so use a deep clone or a deep merge instead.

think.q:
const r = Object.assign({}, "ab", null, [9])
console.log(r)
opts: It throws a TypeError because of null
why: The string becomes an object with the keys "0" and "1". null is skipped. The array [9] then overwrites key "0", while key "1" stays.
Primitive sources are coerced to objects, and a later source wins on a clash.

think.q:
const src = { get x() { return 5 } }
const r = Object.assign({}, src)
console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(r, "x"))
What is r.x in the copy?
opts: A getter, copied from the source
A plain data property with the value 5
A data property with the value undefined
why: Object.assign reads src.x (which runs the getter) and then assigns the result. So the target gets the value 5 at copy time.
To copy getters themselves, use Object.defineProperties with Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors.

think.q:
const a = { n: { v: 1 } }
const c = Object.assign({}, a)
c.n.v = 2
console.log(a.n.v)
why: The copy is shallow. c.n and a.n are the same object, so changing it through one is visible through the other.
Only the top-level property was copied, and its value is a reference. Use a deep clone when you need independent nested data.

think.q:
const s = Symbol("id")
const r = Object.assign({}, { [s]: 1, a: 2 })
console.log(Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(r).length)
opts: 1, because own enumerable Symbol keys are copied too
0, because only string keys are copied
It throws a TypeError for Symbol keys
why: Many people think only string keys are copied. In fact Object.assign copies enumerable own Symbol keys as well. Object.keys alone would miss them.
List them with Object.getOwnPropertySymbols and check that each one is enumerable.

think.q:
const t = { set x(v) { this.log = "set " + v } }
Object.assign(t, { x: 5 })
console.log(t.log)
opts: It throws, because t has no data property x
why: The target is written with a normal assignment (t.x = 5), which calls the setter. A copy made with Object.defineProperty would replace the setter and never call it.
So your version should use target[key] = value.

problems.pseudo:
objectAssign(target, ...sources)
  if target is null or undefined, throw a TypeError
  make sure target is an object (wrap a primitive)
  for each source, in order
    if source is null or undefined, skip it
    make sure source is an object (a string becomes an object of its characters)
    collect its own string keys and its own symbol keys
    keep only the keys that are enumerable
    for each key
      read the value from the source (this runs getters)
      write the value to the target (this runs setters)
  return the target
watch: Which properties should be skipped: inherited ones, hidden (non-enumerable) ones, or both?
Does a normal read and write on the target run getters and setters? Is that what you want here?
What should happen when a source is null, undefined, or a string?

build.problem: Implement objectAssign(target, ...sources) that behaves like Object.assign without calling it.
reqs: Copy own enumerable properties from every source onto the target, and return the target itself.
Later sources overwrite earlier ones.
Skip null and undefined sources. Throw a TypeError for a null or undefined target.
Do not copy inherited or non-enumerable properties.
Read with the source's getters, write with the target's setters, and copy enumerable Symbol keys too.
Coerce primitive sources (for example a string).

checks.t: Copies properties, returns the target, later sources win
checks.verify:
const t = { a: 1 }; const r = objectAssign(t, { b: 2, a: 3 }, { b: 4 });
assert(r === t, 'must return the same target object'); assert(t.a === 3 && t.b === 4, 'later sources must overwrite')
checks.gap: Return the target object that was passed in, not a new object, and loop through the sources in order.

checks.t: null and undefined sources are skipped
checks.test:
const t = objectAssign({}, null, undefined, { a: 1 });
console.log(t); // expected: { a: 1 }
checks.verify: const t = objectAssign({}, null, undefined, { a: 1 }); assert(t.a === 1 && Object.keys(t).length === 1, 'must skip null and undefined sources')
checks.gap: Add if (source == null) continue inside the source loop. Object.keys(null) would throw.

checks.t: Inherited and non-enumerable properties are not copied
checks.verify:
const src = Object.create({ inherited: 1 }); src.own = 2; Object.defineProperty(src, 'hidden', { value: 3, enumerable: false });
const r = objectAssign({}, src); assert(r.own === 2, 'own copied'); assert(!('inherited' in r) && !('hidden' in r), 'inherited and hidden must not be copied')
checks.gap: Do not use for...in (it includes inherited keys). Use Object.keys or check propertyIsEnumerable on own keys.

checks.t: Getters on the source run, and setters on the target run
checks.verify:
let reads = 0; const src = { get x() { reads++; return 5 } }; const t = { set y(v) { this.got = v } };
objectAssign(t, src, { y: 7 }); assert(reads === 1 && t.x === 5, 'source getter must run once and the value be copied'); assert(t.got === 7, 'target setter must run')
checks.gap: Use plain target[key] = source[key]. Copying descriptors with defineProperty skips the target setter.

checks.t: Enumerable Symbol keys are copied
checks.verify: const s = Symbol('id'); const r = objectAssign({}, { [s]: 1, a: 2 }); assert(r[s] === 1 && r.a === 2, 'symbol key must be copied')
checks.gap: Also loop over Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(source) and copy the ones that are enumerable.

checks.t: Primitive sources are coerced; a null target throws
checks.test:
console.log(objectAssign({}, 'ab', 5)); // expected: { 0: 'a', 1: 'b' }
try { objectAssign(null, {}) } catch (e) { console.log(e instanceof TypeError) } // expected: true
checks.verify:
const r = objectAssign({}, 'ab', 5); assert(r[0] === 'a' && r[1] === 'b' && Object.keys(r).length === 2, 'string source must give index keys, number gives nothing');
let ok = false; try { objectAssign(null, {}) } catch (e) { ok = e instanceof TypeError } assert(ok, 'null target must throw TypeError')
checks.gap: Wrap each source with Object(source) before listing keys, and throw a TypeError at the start if the target is null or undefined.

notes: The copy is shallow: nested objects are shared by reference.
Object.keys returns only own enumerable string keys. Symbols need their own step.
to[key] = from[key] is the spec's read-then-write, so getters and setters behave correctly.
null/undefined sources are skipped, but a null/undefined target is an error.
Spreading { ...a, ...b } is similar, but it defines properties instead of calling target setters.
next: Write deepMerge(target, ...sources) that merges nested plain objects instead of replacing them.
Explain why Object.assign(obj, JSON.parse(userInput)) with a __proto__ key can be dangerous.

what: Array.from creates a real array from something that is not one yet. It accepts two kinds of input: iterables (strings, Sets, Maps, generators, anything with Symbol.iterator) and array-like objects (objects with a length and numbered keys, such as { 0: "a", 1: "b", length: 2 }).
An optional mapFn transforms every item while the array is built, so Array.from(x, fn) works like Array.from(x).map(fn) but in one pass. The function gets (value, index).
If an object is both iterable and array-like, the iterator wins.
Think of a conveyor belt that delivers items one by one (an iterable) or a numbered shelf where you pick items by position (array-like). Either way, you put the items into a proper box: an array.

steps: Reject null and undefined with a TypeError. If mapFn is given, it must be a function.
Check whether the input has a Symbol.iterator method.
If yes, walk it with for...of and add each value to a new array (mapped, if mapFn exists).
If not, read length (turn it into a safe non-negative whole number) and read items[0] up to items[length - 1].
Return the new array. The input is never changed.
how.diagram:
Iterable:      "a😀"   -> for...of -> ["a", "😀"]   (2 items)

Array-like:    { 0: "x", 1: "y", length: 2 }
               i = 0..1 -> items[i] -> ["x", "y"]

Length only:   { length: 3 } with mapFn (_, i) => i * 2
               -> [0, 2, 4]

where: Array.from(document.querySelectorAll("li")) gives you map and filter on a NodeList.
Turn new Set(list) back into an array to remove duplicates.
Strings are split into code points, not into UTF-16 units, so emoji stay in one piece.

think.q: Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i * 2)
opts: It throws, because the object is not iterable
why: An object with only length: 3 is array-like. Reading missing indexes gives undefined items, and the map function receives each index, so the result is [0, 2, 4].
Without the map function you would get three undefined values.

think.q: Which expression gives 2 for the string "a😀"?
why: The emoji takes two UTF-16 units, so .length and split("") both give 3 and cut the emoji in half.
Strings are iterable by code point, and Array.from uses the iterator, so you get 2 items.

think.q:
const o = {
  length: 5,
  *[Symbol.iterator]() { yield "x" }
}
Array.from(o)
opts: It throws, because the object is ambiguous
["x"], because the iterator is checked first
why: If the input has a Symbol.iterator method, Array.from uses it and ignores length.
This is why the iterable check must come before the length-based loop.

think.q: Array.from([10, 20], function () { return arguments.length })
why: The map function of Array.from is called with (value, index) only. Unlike Array.prototype.map, it does not receive the array as a third argument.
If your version passes three arguments, the output becomes [3, 3].

think.q:
Array.from({ length: -3 })
What is returned?
why: The length is converted to a whole number and then clamped to a minimum of 0. Negative, NaN and missing lengths all become 0.
A loop like for (i = 0; i < length; i++) already does nothing for a negative length, but new Array(-3) would throw. Do not allocate with the raw length.

problems.pseudo:
arrayFrom(items, mapFn, thisArg)
  if items is null or undefined, throw a TypeError
  if mapFn was given and is not a function, throw a TypeError
  make an empty result list
  define "convert(value, index)"
    if mapFn exists, return mapFn called with thisArg, value, index
    otherwise return value
  if items has an iterator method
    for each value produced by the iterator
      add convert(value, its position) to the result
  otherwise (array-like)
    read items' length
    turn it into a whole number, minimum 0
    for each position from 0 up to length - 1
      add convert(items at that position, position) to the result
  return the result
watch: Which check comes first when an object is both iterable and array-like?
What if length is missing, negative, a string, or NaN?
Which arguments does the map function get, and with which this?

build.problem: Implement arrayFrom(items, mapFn?, thisArg?) that builds a new array from an iterable or an array-like object, without calling Array.from.
reqs: Work with array-like objects (length plus indexed items).
Work with iterables (Symbol.iterator), including strings, Sets and generators.
Apply the optional mapFn(value, index) with thisArg as this.
Always return a new array and never change the input.
Handle empty inputs and bad lengths. Throw a TypeError for null/undefined or a non-function mapFn.

checks.t: Converts an array-like object
checks.test: console.log(arrayFrom({ 0: 'a', 1: 'b', length: 2 })); // expected: ['a', 'b']
checks.verify: const r = arrayFrom({ 0: 'a', 1: 'b', length: 2 }); assert(Array.isArray(r) && r.join() === 'a,b', 'array-like must be converted')
checks.gap: For input without an iterator, read length and loop from 0 to length - 1 reading items[i].

checks.t: Converts iterables (Set, string, generator)
checks.test:
console.log(arrayFrom(new Set([1, 2, 2, 3])), arrayFrom('a😀'), arrayFrom((function* () { yield 7 })()));
// expected: [1, 2, 3] ['a', '😀'] [7]
checks.verify:
assert(arrayFrom(new Set([1, 2, 2, 3])).join() === '1,2,3', 'Set'); const s = arrayFrom('a😀'); assert(s.length === 2 && s[1] === '😀', 'string by code point');
assert(arrayFrom((function* () { yield 7 })()).join() === '7', 'generator')
checks.gap: Check typeof items[Symbol.iterator] === "function" and use for...of. Do not rely on length for strings.

checks.t: mapFn gets (value, index) and thisArg
checks.test:
const r = arrayFrom([5, 6], function (v, i) { return v + i + this.k + arguments.length }, { k: 100 });
console.log(r); // expected: [107, 109]
checks.verify:
const r = arrayFrom([5, 6], function (v, i) { return v + i + this.k + arguments.length }, { k: 100 });
assert(r[0] === 107 && r[1] === 109, 'mapFn must get exactly (value, index) and the given this')
checks.gap: Call mapFn.call(thisArg, value, index) with two arguments only. Do not pass the array as a third argument.

checks.t: Returns a new array and does not change the input
checks.test:
const a = [1, 2]; const r = arrayFrom(a);
console.log(r !== a, a); // expected: true [1, 2]
checks.verify: const a = [1, 2]; const r = arrayFrom(a); assert(r !== a && r.join() === '1,2' && a.length === 2, 'must be a new array and input unchanged')
checks.gap: Create a new empty array for the result and push into it. Do not return the input.

checks.t: Length-only objects and bad lengths
checks.test:
console.log(arrayFrom({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i * 2), arrayFrom({ length: -3 }), arrayFrom({ length: '2', 0: 'x' }), arrayFrom({}));
// expected: [0, 2, 4] [] ['x', undefined] []
checks.gap: Convert the length with Math.trunc(Number(len)) || 0 and clamp it to at least 0 before looping.

checks.t: Iterator wins over length
checks.test:
const o = { length: 5, *[Symbol.iterator]() { yield 'x' } };
console.log(arrayFrom(o)); // expected: ['x']
checks.verify: const o = { length: 5, *[Symbol.iterator]() { yield 'x' } }; const r = arrayFrom(o); assert(r.length === 1 && r[0] === 'x', 'iterator must be used before length')
checks.gap: Test for the iterator first. Only fall back to the length loop when there is no Symbol.iterator.

checks.t: Bad arguments throw a TypeError
checks.verify:
let a = false; try { arrayFrom(null) } catch (e) { a = e instanceof TypeError } assert(a, 'null input');
let b = false; try { arrayFrom([1], 'nope') } catch (e) { b = e instanceof TypeError } assert(b, 'non-function mapFn')
checks.gap: Validate at the start: items == null is an error, and mapFn must be undefined or a function.

notes: Two paths: iterate when Symbol.iterator exists, otherwise loop over length. The iterator path must come first.
Cleaning the length with Math.trunc(Number(...)) || 0 handles strings, NaN and negatives.
The map function gets exactly (value, index) and the optional thisArg.
Missing indexes in an array-like object read as undefined, so they become undefined items.
The input is only read, and the result is always a fresh array.
next: Add a guard for huge lengths so that a bad length cannot freeze the page.
Implement Array.of and explain how it differs from new Array(3).

what: find walks through an array from the start and returns the first item for which your callback returns a truthy value. If no item matches, it returns undefined.
It stops as soon as it finds a match, so the rest of the array is never visited. The callback receives (item, index, array), and an optional thisArg becomes this inside a regular function callback.
One detail surprises many people: find does visit empty slots of a sparse array and treats them as undefined. Methods such as map, filter and forEach skip them.
Think of looking for your keys by checking each pocket in order. You stop as soon as you find them. If every pocket is empty, you come back with nothing.

steps: Check that the callback is a function. If not, throw a TypeError.
Read the length once before the loop starts.
For each index from 0 to length - 1, read the item (an empty slot reads as undefined).
Call the callback with (item, index, array) and the right this.
If the result is truthy, return the item immediately. After the loop, return undefined.
how.diagram:
[5, 8, 12, 3].find(n => n > 6)

i=0  5   5 > 6 ? no
i=1  8   8 > 6 ? yes  -> return 8      (12 and 3 are never visited)

[1, , 3].find(...)   visits i=0, i=1 (hole -> undefined), i=2

where: users.find(u => u.id === id) returns the matching user object.
Find the first enabled option, or the first error in a list of validation results.
Pick the selected tab or the first visible item from a list.
If an item can itself be undefined, a result of undefined is ambiguous. Use findIndex in that case.

think.q:
let n = 0
[1, , 3].find(() => { n++; return false })
console.log(n)
why: find visits every index, including the empty slot, which it reads as undefined. So the callback runs 3 times.
With filter or forEach, you would get 2. Do not add an i in arr check to find.

think.q: The array is [undefined, 5]. arr.find(x => x === undefined) returns undefined. What is the best way to know whether a match was found?
opts: Use findIndex, because it returns -1 when nothing matches
why: A found undefined and "not found" look the same in the result of find. findIndex returns the position (or -1), so it cannot be confused.
The trap is thinking undefined always means "no match".

think.q:
let calls = 0
const r = [1, 2, 3, 4].find((x) => { calls++; return x > 1 })
console.log(calls, r)
why: The callback sees 1 (false) and then 2 (true). find returns immediately, so the callback is never called for 3 and 4.
If you build find with filter(...)[0], you lose this early exit.

think.q:
[5].find(function () { return this.ok }, { ok: true })
What is returned, and what changes if the callback becomes an arrow function () => this.ok?
opts: 5 for the regular function. An arrow function ignores thisArg, so this.ok comes from the outer scope
why: The callback returns a truthy value, so the item (5) is returned, never the callback result. Arrow functions have no this of their own, so call(thisArg, ...) cannot change it.
Always use callback.call(thisArg, item, i, arr).

think.q:
const a = [1, 2]
a.find((x) => { if (a.length < 5) a.push(x); return false })
console.log(a.length)
why: The length is read once before the loop, so only the original two indexes are visited. The callback pushes twice, giving a final length of 4. Items added during the walk are not visited.
If you re-read arr.length in every loop test, the loop would run until the length reaches 5.

problems.pseudo:
arr.myFind(callback, thisArg)
  if the array is null or undefined, throw a TypeError
  if callback is not a function, throw a TypeError
  read the array's length once and remember it
  for each position from 0 up to length - 1
    read the item at that position (a hole reads as undefined)
    call callback with thisArg as "this" and (item, position, array)
    if the result is truthy
      return the item
  return undefined (nothing matched)
watch: Do you return the item, the index, or the callback result when it matches?
Should an empty slot in the array be skipped or visited?
Is the length read once before the loop, or on every step?

build.problem: Implement Array.prototype.myFind(callback, thisArg) without using find, filter or similar built-ins.
reqs: Return the first item for which the callback returns a truthy value.
Return undefined when nothing matches.
Call the callback with (item, index, array) and thisArg as this.
Stop as soon as a match is found.
Visit empty slots in sparse arrays as undefined, like the built-in find.
Throw a TypeError if the callback is not a function.

checks.t: Returns the first matching item
checks.test: console.log([5, 8, 12, 3].myFind(n => n > 6)); // expected: 8
checks.verify: assert([5, 8, 12, 3].myFind(n => n > 6) === 8, 'must return the first match')
checks.gap: Return arr[i] (the item) as soon as the callback is truthy. Do not return the index or the callback result.

checks.t: Returns undefined when nothing matches
checks.test: console.log([1, 2].myFind(n => n > 5), [].myFind(() => true)); // expected: undefined undefined
checks.verify: assert([1, 2].myFind(n => n > 5) === undefined && [].myFind(() => true) === undefined, 'no match gives undefined')
checks.gap: After the loop ends, return undefined explicitly. Make sure an empty array just skips the loop.

checks.t: The callback receives (item, index, array)
checks.verify: const a = ['x', 'y']; let seen = ''; a.myFind((v, i, arr) => { seen += v + i + (arr === a); return false }); assert(seen === 'x0truey1true', 'callback must get item, index and array')
checks.gap: Call callback.call(thisArg, arr[i], i, arr) with all three arguments.

checks.t: thisArg is used for regular functions
checks.test: console.log([5].myFind(function () { return this.ok }, { ok: true })); // expected: 5
checks.verify: assert([5].myFind(function () { return this.ok }, { ok: true }) === 5, 'thisArg must be this inside the callback')
checks.gap: Use callback.call(thisArg, ...) or apply. A plain callback(...) call loses this.

checks.t: Stops at the first match
checks.verify: let calls = 0; [1, 2, 3, 4].myFind(x => { calls++; return x > 1 }); assert(calls === 2, 'must stop after the first match')
checks.gap: Return from inside the loop. Do not collect all matches first and take the first one.

checks.t: Empty slots are visited as undefined
checks.verify:
let n = 0; [1, , 3].myFind(() => { n++; return false }); assert(n === 3, 'holes must be visited');
assert([1, , 3].myFind(x => x === undefined) === undefined, 'hole is seen as undefined')
checks.gap: Use a plain index loop without an i in arr check. Unlike map or forEach, find reads holes as undefined.

checks.t: Items added during the search are not visited; bad callback throws
checks.verify:
const a = [1, 2]; a.myFind(x => { a.push(x); return false }); assert(a.length === 4, 'length must be read once');
let ok = false; try { [1].myFind('nope') } catch (e) { ok = e instanceof TypeError } assert(ok, 'non-function must throw TypeError')
checks.gap: Store const len = arr.length before the loop and use it in the loop test. Add a typeof callback !== "function" check at the top.

notes: A plain index loop with an early return is all you need. That is what gives the early exit.
Reading arr[i] for a hole gives undefined, which is exactly what find should see.
The length is read once, so items pushed during the loop are not visited.
callback.call(thisArg, item, i, arr) supplies the three arguments and the this value.
arr.length >>> 0 turns the length into an unsigned whole number, the same trick the spec uses.
next: Write some and every and decide whether they should skip holes (check the spec).
Implement myFind for array-like objects with Array.prototype.myFind.call(obj, fn).

what: includes answers a yes/no question: "is this value somewhere in the array?". It returns true or false, never an index.

Its comparison rule is called SameValueZero. It is almost the same as ===, with one big difference: NaN is considered equal to NaN. And +0 and -0 are equal, as with ===. That is why [NaN].includes(NaN) is true while [NaN].indexOf(NaN) is -1.
The optional fromIndex says where to start. A negative number counts from the end, and a number below -length simply starts at the beginning.

Think of checking a guest list for a name. You can start at the top, or you can start from a line near the end. Two "Unknown" guests count as the same person, even though normally "not a number" never equals itself.

steps: If the array is empty, return false right away.
Turn fromIndex into a whole number. A missing or invalid value means 0.
If it is negative, add the array length, and use 0 if that is still negative. If it is at or past the end, nothing is left to search.
Walk from that index to the end and compare each item with SameValueZero.
Return true on the first match, or false after the loop.
how.diagram:
[1, 2, NaN, 4].includes(NaN)        -> true   (NaN equals NaN here)
[1, 2, 3].includes(3, -1)           -> true   start = 3 + -1 = 2
[1, 2, 3].includes(1, -2)           -> false  start = 1, skips the 1
[1, 2, 3].includes(1, -99)          -> true   start clamped to 0
[1, 2, 3].includes(3, 5)            -> false  nothing left to search

SameValueZero(a, b):  a === b  OR  (a is NaN AND b is NaN)

where: ["admin", "editor"].includes(role) is the common way to check permissions or allowed values.
Check whether a list of selected ids already contains an id before adding it.
Check numbers that might be NaN, where indexOf would fail.
Objects are compared by reference, so [{ a: 1 }].includes({ a: 1 }) is false.

think.q: console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN), [NaN].includes(NaN))
why: indexOf uses strict equality, and NaN === NaN is false, so it never finds NaN. includes uses SameValueZero, which treats two NaN values as equal.
So this.indexOf(x) !== -1 is not a correct way to write includes.

think.q: console.log([0].includes(-0), Object.is(0, -0))
why: SameValueZero treats +0 and -0 as equal, so includes finds it. Object.is distinguishes them.
So you cannot use Object.is as the comparison. You need === plus a special case for NaN.

think.q: console.log([1, 2, 3].includes(1, -2))
why: A negative fromIndex counts from the end: 3 + (-2) = 1. The search starts at index 1, so the 1 at index 0 is skipped.
The trap is reading -2 as "the last two items are skipped" or as "ignore it".

think.q: console.log([1, , 3].includes(undefined), [1, , 3].indexOf(undefined))
why: includes reads every index, and an empty slot reads as undefined, so it finds it. indexOf skips empty slots and returns -1.
So your loop should not check i in arr.

think.q: A version only handles a negative index like this: if (from < 0) from = len + from. What goes wrong for [1, 2, 3].includes(undefined, -100)?
opts: The start becomes -97. Reading arr[-97] gives undefined, which matches, so it wrongly returns true
It always returns false for negative numbers
why: After adding the length, the start is still negative, so the loop begins at -97 and reads arr[-97], arr[-96] and so on. These positions do not exist and read as undefined, so a search for undefined matches by mistake.
Clamp with Math.max(0, len + from). The correct answer is false, because no item in the array is undefined.

problems.pseudo:
arr.myIncludes(search, fromIndex)
  if the array is null or undefined, throw a TypeError
  read the length
  if the length is 0, return false
  turn fromIndex into a whole number (missing or invalid means 0)
  if the number is not negative
    start = that number
  otherwise
    start = length + that number, but never below 0
  for each position from start up to length - 1
    read the item (a hole reads as undefined)
    if item equals search by strict equality
      return true
    if both item and search are NaN
      return true
  return false
watch: How can you recognise NaN, if NaN === NaN is false?
What start index do you use for -1, for -100, and for a number larger than the length?
Should empty slots be skipped, or compared as undefined?

build.problem: Implement Array.prototype.myIncludes(searchElement, fromIndex) using SameValueZero, without using includes or indexOf.
reqs: Return true if the value is found, otherwise false.
Compare with SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and 0 equals -0.
A negative fromIndex counts from the end, and the start never goes below 0.
A fromIndex at or past the length returns false.
Treat empty slots as undefined, and never change the array.

checks.t: Finds and does not find values with strict equality
checks.gap: Use === for the comparison. Do not use ==, and do not compare object contents.

checks.t: NaN is found
checks.test: console.log([1, NaN].myIncludes(NaN), [1, 2].myIncludes(NaN)); // expected: true false
checks.verify: assert([1, NaN].myIncludes(NaN) === true, 'NaN must be found'); assert([1, 2].myIncludes(NaN) === false, 'NaN must not be found when absent')
checks.gap: NaN is the only value not equal to itself. Add a second test: item !== item && search !== search (or Number.isNaN for both).

checks.t: 0 and -0 are equal
checks.test: console.log([0].myIncludes(-0), [-0].myIncludes(0)); // expected: true true
checks.verify: assert([0].myIncludes(-0) === true && [-0].myIncludes(0) === true, '+0 and -0 must be equal')
checks.gap: Do not use Object.is, which separates +0 and -0. Plain === already treats them as equal.

checks.t: A positive fromIndex skips earlier items
checks.test: console.log([1, 2, 3].myIncludes(1, 1), [1, 2, 3].myIncludes(3, 2), [1, 2, 3].myIncludes(3, 3)); // expected: false true false
checks.verify:
assert([1, 2, 3].myIncludes(1, 1) === false, 'item before fromIndex must be skipped'); assert([1, 2, 3].myIncludes(3, 2) === true, 'item at fromIndex counts');
assert([1, 2, 3].myIncludes(3, 3) === false && [1, 2, 3].myIncludes(3, 99) === false, 'start at or past the end finds nothing')
checks.gap: Start the loop at fromIndex. If it is not less than the length the loop does not run, so the answer is false.

checks.t: A negative fromIndex counts from the end and is clamped at 0
checks.test: console.log([1, 2, 3].myIncludes(1, -2), [1, 2, 3].myIncludes(3, -1), [1, 2, 3].myIncludes(1, -99)); // expected: false true true
checks.verify:
assert([1, 2, 3].myIncludes(1, -2) === false, '-2 starts at index 1'); assert([1, 2, 3].myIncludes(3, -1) === true, '-1 starts at index 2');
assert([1, 2, 3].myIncludes(1, -99) === true, 'too negative starts at 0')
checks.gap: Compute Math.max(0, length + fromIndex) for a negative fromIndex.

checks.t: Empty slots are seen as undefined
checks.test: console.log([1, , 3].myIncludes(undefined), [1, 2].myIncludes(undefined)); // expected: true false
checks.verify: assert([1, , 3].myIncludes(undefined) === true, 'hole counts as undefined'); assert([1, 2].myIncludes(undefined) === false, 'absent undefined')
checks.gap: Loop over every index and read arr[i]. Do not skip a position with an i in arr check.

checks.t: Missing or invalid fromIndex means 0; empty array is false
checks.test: console.log([1, 2].myIncludes(1, undefined), [1, 2].myIncludes(1, 'x'), [].myIncludes(undefined)); // expected: true true false
checks.verify: assert([1, 2].myIncludes(1, undefined) === true && [1, 2].myIncludes(1, 'x') === true, 'invalid fromIndex must act like 0'); assert([].myIncludes(undefined) === false, 'empty array is false')
checks.gap: Convert with Math.trunc(Number(fromIndex)) || 0. That makes undefined and NaN become 0.

notes: SameValueZero is === plus "both are NaN". The check x !== x is only true for NaN.
+0 === -0 is already true, so no special case is needed for zero.
Normalise fromIndex once: whole number, default 0, negative counted from the end and clamped at 0.
Reading arr[i] for a hole gives undefined, which matches the behaviour of includes.
A start index at or after the length makes the loop skip, so the function falls through to false.
next: Implement indexOf and lastIndexOf and explain why they cannot find NaN.
Write includesDeep(arr, value) that compares objects by content.
Make a Set-based version that checks membership in constant time, and discuss when to use it.

problems.signature: str.myStartsWith(search, position?) · str.myEndsWith(search, endPosition?) · str.myIncludes(search, position?)

what: startsWith, endsWith and includes answer simple yes/no questions about a piece of text: does it begin with this, end with this, or contain this somewhere?

They are case-sensitive and have two details that people often miss. The search value is converted to a string first, so "null is odd".startsWith(null) is true. And a regular expression is rejected with a TypeError, because it is probably a mistake (you want test or match for patterns).

The optional position moves the window: position (for startsWith and includes) says where to start, and endPosition (for endsWith) says where the text should be treated as if it ended. Numbers outside the text are clamped, never an error.
Think of reading a sentence through a small window. You check the first words in the window, the last words, or any words inside.

steps: Convert the text (this) and the search value to strings. If the search value is a RegExp, throw a TypeError.
Turn the position into a whole number and clamp it between 0 and the text length. A missing position means 0 (or the text length for endsWith).
startsWith: take the piece of text that starts at the position and is as long as the search value. Compare it to the search value.
endsWith: find the start by subtracting the search length from the end. If the start is below 0, return false. Otherwise compare that piece.
includes: look for the search value starting from the position.
how.diagram:
text = "hello world"      (length 11)

startsWith("world", 6)   piece [6, 11) = "world"      -> true
endsWith("hello", 5)     piece [0, 5)  = "hello"      -> true
includes("o w")          found at index 4             -> true

startsWith("", 99)       position clamped to 11, "" = ""  -> true
endsWith("hello world!") start = 11 - 12 < 0             -> false

where: Check a prefix such as "Bearer " before cutting it off.
Pattern matching (digits, optional parts, case-insensitive). Use a regular expression with test instead.

think.q: console.log("abc".startsWith(""), "abc".includes("", 99), "abc".endsWith(""))
why: An empty string is found at every position, including the very end, so all three are true. The position 99 is clamped to the text length, which is still a valid place to find an empty string.
Do not return false just because the search value is empty or the position is large.

think.q: console.log("undefined is a word".startsWith())
opts: It throws a TypeError, because nothing was passed
why: A missing argument is undefined, and the search value is converted to the string "undefined". The text starts with those letters, so the result is true.
Only regular expressions are rejected. Everything else is converted with String(...).

think.q: Why does "a.b".includes(/./) throw a TypeError instead of searching with the pattern?
opts: The language wants to avoid a silent mistake: people may think a pattern is used, while a plain text search is done on the text of the pattern
why: Without the guard, the pattern would be converted to the string "/./" and searched as plain text. That would quietly give the wrong answer.
The explicit error tells the developer to use regex.test(text) instead.

think.q: console.log("hello world".endsWith("hello", 5))
opts: false, because the text does not end with "hello"
true, because the text is treated as if it ended at position 5
why: For endsWith the second argument is the end position. The text is read as "hello" (the first 5 characters), and that ends with "hello".
This differs from startsWith, where the second argument is the start.

think.q: A version of startsWith does this.slice(pos, pos + search.length) === search but never clamps pos. What happens for "abc".startsWith("a", -1)?
opts: It returns false, because slice(-1, 0) counts from the end and gives an empty string. The built-in clamps to 0 and returns true
why: Negative numbers mean "from the end" for slice, but for these string methods a negative position simply means 0.
Clamp first: Math.min(Math.max(pos, 0), length), then slice.

problems.pseudo:
helper: prepare(text, search)
  if text is null or undefined, throw a TypeError
  if search is a regular expression, throw a TypeError
  convert both to strings

clamp(number, length)
  turn the number into a whole number (invalid means 0)
  keep it between 0 and length

startsWith(search, position)
  start = clamp(position, text length)
  take the piece of text from start, as long as the search string
  return whether that piece equals the search string

endsWith(search, endPosition)
  end = text length if endPosition was not given, otherwise clamp(endPosition)
  start = end - length of search string
  if start is below 0, return false
  return whether the piece from start to end equals the search string

includes(search, position)
  start = clamp(position, text length)
  look for the search string from start
  return whether it was found
watch: What should happen when the position is negative, or bigger than the text?
In endsWith, is the second argument a start or an end, and what is its default?
Which kinds of values must be converted to a string, and which must throw?

build.problem: Implement String.prototype.myStartsWith, myEndsWith and myIncludes without using the built-in startsWith, endsWith or includes.
reqs: myStartsWith(search, position = 0) checks the text from position.
myEndsWith(search, endPosition = length) treats the text as ending at endPosition.
myIncludes(search, position = 0) looks for the search value from position.
Convert the search value to a string, and throw a TypeError if it is a regular expression.
Clamp positions into the text. Out-of-range positions never throw. Comparison is case-sensitive.

checks.t: myStartsWith works with and without a position
checks.test:
console.log('hello world'.myStartsWith('hello'), 'hello world'.myStartsWith('world', 6), 'hello'.myStartsWith('Hello'), 'hello'.myStartsWith('lo', 1));
// expected: true true false false
checks.verify:
assert('hello world'.myStartsWith('hello') === true, 'prefix'); assert('hello world'.myStartsWith('world', 6) === true, 'with position');
assert('hello'.myStartsWith('Hello') === false, 'case-sensitive'); assert('hello'.myStartsWith('lo', 1) === false, 'must match at the position')
checks.gap: Compare the slice text.slice(pos, pos + search.length) with the search string. Do not use a case-insensitive comparison.

checks.t: myEndsWith uses the end position
checks.test:
console.log('hello world'.myEndsWith('world'), 'hello world'.myEndsWith('hello', 5), 'hello'.myEndsWith('hello!'));
// expected: true true false
checks.verify:
assert('hello world'.myEndsWith('world') === true, 'suffix'); assert('hello world'.myEndsWith('hello', 5) === true, 'end position');
assert('hello'.myEndsWith('hello!') === false, 'longer search value must be false')
checks.gap: Compute end (default: length) and start = end - search.length. If start < 0 return false. Compare slice(start, end).

checks.t: myIncludes finds text at or after the position
checks.test:
console.log('hello'.myIncludes('ell'), 'hello'.myIncludes('ell', 2), 'hello'.myIncludes('xyz'));
// expected: true false false
checks.verify: assert('hello'.myIncludes('ell') === true, 'found'); assert('hello'.myIncludes('ell', 2) === false, 'before the position'); assert('hello'.myIncludes('xyz') === false, 'absent')
checks.gap: Start looking at position. A simple way is a loop that checks each start index, or indexOf(search, position) !== -1.

checks.t: An empty search string is always found
checks.test:
console.log(''.myStartsWith(''), 'abc'.myEndsWith(''), 'abc'.myIncludes('', 99), 'abc'.myStartsWith('', 99));
// expected: true true true true
checks.verify:
assert(''.myStartsWith('') === true && 'abc'.myEndsWith('') === true, 'empty prefix/suffix');
assert('abc'.myIncludes('', 99) === true && 'abc'.myStartsWith('', 99) === true, 'empty search with a big position')
checks.gap: After clamping, the position is at most the text length, and an empty piece equals an empty search. Do not special-case "position too large" into false.

checks.t: Positions are clamped, never an error
checks.test:
console.log('abc'.myStartsWith('a', -5), 'abc'.myEndsWith('c', 99), 'abc'.myEndsWith('a', -1), 'abc'.myIncludes('c', 99));
// expected: true true false false
checks.verify:
assert('abc'.myStartsWith('a', -5) === true, 'negative position acts like 0'); assert('abc'.myEndsWith('c', 99) === true, 'big end position acts like length');
assert('abc'.myEndsWith('a', -1) === false, 'negative end position acts like 0'); assert('abc'.myIncludes('c', 99) === false, 'start past the end finds nothing')
checks.gap: Clamp every position with Math.min(Math.max(n, 0), length) before slicing. Negative values must not be passed to slice.

checks.t: The search value is converted to a string
checks.test:
console.log('null is odd'.myStartsWith(null), '1234'.myIncludes(23), 'undefined!'.myStartsWith());
// expected: true true true
checks.verify:
assert('null is odd'.myStartsWith(null) === true, 'null becomes "null"'); assert('1234'.myIncludes(23) === true, 'number becomes string');
assert('undefined!'.myStartsWith() === true, 'missing argument becomes "undefined"')
checks.gap: Use String(search) once at the start of every method.

checks.t: A RegExp search value throws a TypeError
checks.gap: Before converting to a string, check search instanceof RegExp and throw new TypeError(...).

notes: One shared prepare step converts to strings and rejects regular expressions, so all three methods behave the same.
Clamp before slicing. Negative numbers passed to slice count from the end, which is not what we want.
endsWith has a different default and meaning for its second argument: it is the end of the window, not the start.
An empty search string matches at every valid position, including the end of the text.
The loop for includes stops when the remaining text is shorter than the search string.
next: Make myIncludes faster with an indexOf-style first-character check, or implement the KMP algorithm.
Support case-insensitive versions with an options argument, and explain why toLowerCase can fail for some languages.

what: Object.create(proto) makes a new, empty object whose prototype is proto. The new object has no properties of its own, but it can use everything its prototype has. Reading obj.greet walks up the chain: first the object itself, then proto, then its prototype, and so on.

You can pass null as the prototype to get an object with no inherited properties at all. It has no toString and no hasOwnProperty, which makes it a clean dictionary. The prototype must be an object or null, otherwise it throws a TypeError.
The optional second argument is a map of property descriptors, the same format as Object.defineProperties. Properties added this way are not writable, enumerable or configurable unless you say so.
Think of a new employee who has no personal toolbox, but is allowed to borrow everything from their team's shared toolbox (the prototype).

steps: Check proto. It must be an object, a function, or null. Anything else (a number, a string, undefined) throws a TypeError.
Create a new empty object.
Set its prototype to proto. For null this removes the default Object.prototype.
If a properties object was given, define each property on the new object with its descriptor.
Return the new object.
how.diagram:
const animal = { speak() { return 'sound' } }
const dog = Object.create(animal)

dog ----------> animal ----------> Object.prototype -> null
(no own keys)   speak()

dog.speak()   found on animal -> 'sound'
'speak' in dog              -> true
dog.hasOwnProperty('speak') -> false

where: Child.prototype = Object.create(Parent.prototype) was the standard way to inherit before class.
Object.create(null) avoids clashes with keys like "constructor" or "toString".
Create an object that borrows behaviour from a shared template object.
Changing the prototype later is slow and can confuse engines. Set it once when you create the object.

think.q:
const base = { greet() { return "hi" } }
const o = Object.create(base)
console.log(o.hasOwnProperty("greet"), "greet" in o)
why: hasOwnProperty only looks at the object itself. The in operator walks the whole prototype chain, so it finds greet on base.
Objects created with Object.create(proto) start with no own properties.

think.q:
const d = Object.create(null)
d.a = 1
console.log("" + d)
why: Turning an object into text calls its toString or valueOf, but a null-prototype object has neither, so JavaScript cannot convert it and throws "Cannot convert object to primitive value".
This is the price of having a truly empty object. Use JSON.stringify or Object.keys when you need to print one.

think.q:
const o = Object.create({}, { x: { value: 1 } })
o.x = 2
console.log(o.x, Object.keys(o))
why: A descriptor that does not set writable, enumerable and configurable uses false for all of them. So the assignment is ignored (silently in sloppy mode), and Object.keys does not list the property.
This differs from creating a property by assignment, which makes all three true.

think.q:
function Parent() {}
function Child() {}
Child.prototype = Parent.prototype
Child.prototype.extra = function () { return 1 }
console.log(typeof new Parent().extra)
why: Assigning Parent.prototype directly makes both constructors share one prototype object. Adding a method for Child also adds it to Parent.
Child.prototype = Object.create(Parent.prototype) creates a new object that only inherits from it.

think.q:
function Parent() {}
function Child() {}
Child.prototype = Object.create(Parent.prototype)
console.log(new Child().constructor === Child)
why: The new prototype object is empty, so it has no constructor property of its own. The lookup continues to Parent.prototype, which says Parent.
After using Object.create this way, restore it: Child.prototype.constructor = Child.

problems.pseudo:
objectCreate(proto, propertiesObject)
  if proto is not null, and is not an object or a function
    throw a TypeError
  make a new empty object
  set the new object's prototype to proto
    (null gives an object with no inherited properties)
  if propertiesObject was given
    define every property from it on the new object
      using its descriptors
  return the new object
  // alternative: use a temporary constructor function,
  // point its prototype at proto, and create an instance
  // (this does not work for null)
watch: Which values are allowed as the prototype, and which should throw?
How do you create an object with no prototype at all?
What happens to writable, enumerable and configurable when a descriptor does not mention them?

build.problem: Implement objectCreate(proto, propertiesObject) that behaves like Object.create, without calling it.
reqs: Return a new object whose prototype is proto.
Allow null as the prototype (an object with no prototype chain).
Throw a TypeError if proto is not an object, a function or null.
If propertiesObject is given, define its properties with descriptors, like Object.defineProperties.
The result must work for Child.prototype = objectCreate(Parent.prototype).

checks.t: The prototype is set and nothing is copied onto the object
checks.verify:
const proto = { hi() { return 'hi' } }; const o = objectCreate(proto);
assert(Object.getPrototypeOf(o) === proto, 'prototype must be proto'); assert(o.hi() === 'hi', 'inherited method must work'); assert(Object.keys(o).length === 0 && !Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(o, 'hi'), 'no own properties')
checks.gap: Create an empty object and set its prototype to proto (for example with Object.setPrototypeOf). Do not copy the properties of proto.

checks.t: null gives an object with no prototype
checks.test:
const o = objectCreate(null);
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(o), 'toString' in o); // expected: null false
checks.verify: const o = objectCreate(null); assert(Object.getPrototypeOf(o) === null, 'prototype must be null'); assert(!('toString' in o), 'must not inherit from Object.prototype')
checks.gap: A plain {} inherits from Object.prototype. For null you must remove it with Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, null). A temporary constructor does not work for null.

checks.t: Invalid prototypes throw a TypeError
checks.gap: Allow only null, objects and functions: proto !== null && typeof proto !== "object" && typeof proto !== "function" means throw. Note that undefined must also throw.

checks.t: propertiesObject defines properties with descriptors
checks.verify:
const o = objectCreate({}, { x: { value: 1 }, y: { value: 2, enumerable: true, writable: true } }); try { o.x = 5 } catch {} o.y = 6;
assert(o.x === 1, 'x is not writable by default'); assert(o.y === 6, 'y is writable'); assert(Object.keys(o).join() === 'y', 'only enumerable keys are listed')
checks.gap: Pass the descriptors to Object.defineProperties(obj, propertiesObject). Do not assign the values with obj[key] = ..., which makes everything writable and enumerable.

checks.t: Getters in descriptors work and are own properties
checks.test:
const o = objectCreate({ a: 1 }, { double: { get() { return this.a * 2 }, enumerable: true } });
console.log(o.double, Object.keys(o)); // expected: 2 ['double']
checks.verify:
const o = objectCreate({ a: 1 }, { double: { get() { return this.a * 2 }, enumerable: true } });
assert(o.double === 2, 'getter must use the inherited value'); assert(Object.keys(o).join() === 'double', 'defined property is own')
checks.gap: Keep the descriptor as it is (get/set) and let Object.defineProperties handle it.

checks.t: Works for the classic inheritance pattern
checks.gap: The returned object must be a new object whose prototype is A.prototype, not A.prototype itself.

checks.t: A null properties object throws; undefined is ignored
checks.test:
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(objectCreate({}, undefined)) !== null);
try { objectCreate({}, null) } catch (e) { console.log(e instanceof TypeError) } // expected: true, true
checks.verify:
assert(Object.getPrototypeOf(objectCreate({}, undefined)) !== null, 'undefined properties are ignored');
let ok = false; try { objectCreate({}, null) } catch (e) { ok = e instanceof TypeError } assert(ok, 'null properties must throw TypeError')
checks.gap: Only skip the second step when propertiesObject === undefined. For null, let Object.defineProperties throw its TypeError.

notes: Validate first: the prototype is an object, a function or null. Anything else, including undefined, is an error.
Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, null) is what produces a truly prototype-free object.
The older trick uses a temporary constructor (function F() {}; F.prototype = proto; return new F()). It works for every case except null.
Object.defineProperties keeps descriptors intact, so missing flags default to false.
The new object has no own properties until the second argument adds some.
next: Write inherit(Child, Parent) that sets the prototype chain and restores Child.prototype.constructor.
Implement Object.getPrototypeOf and isPrototypeOf logic by walking the chain manually.
Re-write a small class Dog extends Animal example using only constructor functions and objectCreate.
